Definition

Herd immunity (community immunity, population immunity) is the indirect protection from infectious disease that occurs when a large proportion of a population becomes immune to that disease — either through vaccination or prior infection — such that even unvaccinated or non-immune individuals are protected because the disease has little opportunity to spread within the community.

The principle is that when the proportion of immune individuals exceeds a threshold, the effective reproduction number (Re or Rt) falls below 1, and the infection cannot sustain transmission — eventually dying out.

Concept — Reproduction Number & Threshold

  • R₀ (basic reproduction number) — average number of secondary infections from one case in a fully susceptible population.
  • Re = R₀ × (1 – p), where p = proportion immune.
  • Herd immunity threshold (HIT) = 1 – (1/R₀).
Disease R₀ HIT (≥%)
Measles12–1892–95%
Pertussis12–1792–94%
Diphtheria6–783–85%
Polio5–780–86%
Rubella5–780–85%
Mumps4–775–86%
COVID-19 (ancestral)2–360–70% (Delta ~80%, Omicron ~90%+)
Influenza1.5–233–50%

Clinical Significance in Public Health

1. Protection of Vulnerable Individuals Who Cannot Be Vaccinated

  • Infants <6 months (too young for most vaccines).
  • Immunocompromised (HIV, chemotherapy, transplant recipients, primary immunodeficiency).
  • Pregnant women (live vaccines contraindicated).
  • Individuals with severe vaccine allergy (e.g., egg allergy for yellow fever, MMR).
  • Elderly with poor vaccine response.
  • When herd immunity is high, these individuals are protected indirectly.

2. Disease Elimination & Eradication

  • Elimination — zero cases in a defined geographic area (e.g., polio eliminated from India in 2011; measles eliminated from many countries).
  • Eradication — global zero cases — only achieved for smallpox (1980) and rinderpest (2011); polio & Guinea worm on track.
  • Herd immunity is essential — even a single imported case will not spread if Re < 1.
  • Pulse polio immunisation in India achieved >95% coverage → herd immunity → interrupted wild poliovirus transmission.

3. Outbreak Prevention & Control

  • When coverage falls below threshold, outbreaks occur.
  • Measles outbreaks in communities with low MMR coverage (vaccine hesitancy, antivaxx movement).
  • Diphtheria outbreaks — former Soviet Union (1990s); Yemen (recent conflict-related).
  • Coverage gaps create clusters of susceptible individuals.

4. Vaccine Strategy Design

  • Coverage target must exceed HIT for each vaccine-preventable disease.
  • Uniform coverage is more important than average coverage — pockets of low coverage sustain transmission.
  • Pulse campaigns — NIDs for polio; supplementary immunisation activities (SIAs) for measles.
  • Catch-up campaigns — reach missed children.

5. COVID-19 Pandemic & Herd Immunity

  • Initial HIT estimate for COVID-19 was ~60–70%; revised upward with more transmissible variants (Delta ~80%, Omicron >90%).
  • Hybrid immunity (vaccination + prior infection) gives stronger protection.
  • Waning immunity & immune escape variants (Omicron) mean sterilising herd immunity may be unattainable — but herd protection against severe disease remains achievable.
  • Vaccine inequity (high-income vs low-income countries) prolonged the pandemic.

Factors Affecting Herd Immunity

  • R₀ of pathogen — higher R₀ needs higher coverage.
  • Vaccine efficacy — imperfect vaccines need higher coverage; some provide only protection against disease (not infection).
  • Waning immunity — booster doses needed.
  • Uniformity of coverage — clusters of unvaccinated sustain transmission.
  • Pathogen evolution — antigenic drift (influenza), variants (COVID-19) reduce herd immunity.
  • Population mixing patterns — schools, mass gatherings.

Clinical Pearl

Measles is the most contagious human disease — R₀ of 12–18 — meaning one case infects 12–18 susceptibles; herd immunity threshold of 92–95% is required to prevent outbreaks. This explains why measles is the first disease to re-emerge when vaccine coverage falls — even a small dip below 95% leads to outbreaks (e.g., 2019 US outbreaks linked to international travel + pockets of vaccine refusal). The MMR-autism myth (Wakefield 1998, retracted 2010) caused lasting vaccine hesitancy and measles resurgence in the UK, Europe, and US. India's Universal Immunisation Programme (UIP) targets >90% coverage for all vaccines — Mission Indradhanush (since 2014) intensifies efforts in low-coverage districts. The COVID-19 pandemic underscored both the power and limitations of herd immunity — vaccines dramatically reduced severe disease, but Omicron's immune escape means we may never reach true sterilising herd immunity for SARS-CoV-2. The future is herd protection against severe disease through continued vaccination + boosters for high-risk groups, rather than preventing all infection.

Introduction

Fungi are eukaryotic organisms with chitin-containing cell walls and ergosterol-containing cell membranes. Morphologically classified into 4 groups: yeasts, yeast-like fungi, moulds, and dimorphic fungi.

1. Yeasts

  • Unicellular, round/oval (3–8 µm); reproduce asexually by budding (blastogenesis).
  • Colony on SDA — creamy, pasty.
  • Examples: Candida albicans (oral thrush, vulvovaginitis); Cryptococcus neoformans (meningitis in HIV; India ink positive); Malassezia furfur (pityriasis versicolor); Saccharomyces cerevisiae.

2. Yeast-like Fungi

  • Intermediate; grow as yeast at 37 °C, but form pseudohyphae at lower temperatures.
  • Examples: Candida albicans (germ tube positive); C. tropicalis, C. parapsilosis, C. krusei, C. glabrata (non-albicans Candida).

3. Moulds (Filamentous Fungi)

  • Multicellular; grow as branching hyphae (tubular cells); mass of hyphae = mycelium.
  • Two types of hyphae:
    • Septate — cross-walls (septa); e.g., Aspergillus, dermatophytes.
    • Aseptate (coenocytic) — no cross-walls; broad, ribbon-like; e.g., Mucor, Rhizopus (Mucorales).
  • Colony — cottony, woolly, powdery with various pigments.

Subtypes of Moulds

Type Examples Disease
Zygomycetes (Mucorales)Rhizopus, Mucor, AbsidiaRhinocerebral mucormycosis (DKA); angioinvasive
Hyaline septateAspergillus fumigatus, Fusarium, Penicillium marneffeiInvasive aspergillosis, aspergilloma, ABPA, keratitis
Dermatophytes (keratinophilic)Trichophyton, Microsporum, Epidermophyton floccosumTinea (capitis, corporis, cruris, pedis, unguium)
Dematiaceous (pigmented)Alternaria, Cladosporium, Bipolaris, CurvulariaPhaeohyphomycosis, chromoblastomycosis, eumycetoma

4. Dimorphic Fungi

  • Exist as mould at 25 °C (environmental) & yeast (or spherule) at 37 °C (host).
  • Temperature-dependent dimorphism = virulence factor.
Fungus Mould (25 °C) Tissue form (37 °C)
Histoplasma capsulatumTuberculate macroconidiaSmall intracellular yeast (2–4 µm)
Blastomyces dermatitidisPear-shaped conidiaBroad-based budding yeast
Coccidioides immitisArthroconidiaSpherule with endospores
Paracoccidioides brasiliensisChlamydospore-like"Captain's wheel" multiple budding yeast
Sporothrix schenckiiFlower-like conidiaCigar-shaped yeast
Talaromyces (Penicillium) marneffeiBrush conidiophoreFission yeast (transverse septum)

Special Mention — Pneumocystis jirovecii

Originally classified as protozoan (Pneumocystis carinii); now recognised as a fungus based on rRNA & ergosterol synthesis. Cysts seen on silver stain (GMS) in bronchoalveolar lavage — "crushed ping-pong balls". Causes PCP pneumonia in HIV (CD4 <200). Does not grow on SDA.

Clinical Pearl

The single most important bedside clue to fungal morphology is the KOH mount with calcofluor white: yeasts = oval budding cells; pseudohyphae = constrictions at septa (like sausages); true hyphae = parallel walls & true septa; aseptate (Mucorales) hyphae = broad (6–15 µm), ribbon-like, branching at 90°. This distinction is critical — Mucorales require urgent liposomal amphotericin B + surgical debridement (poor response to voriconazole, first-line for Aspergillus). The COVID-19 pandemic saw a surge of COVID-associated mucormycosis (CAM) in India — uncontrolled diabetes, steroid therapy, iron overload. Remember: hyaline septate acute-angle branching = Aspergillus; broad aseptate right-angle branching = Mucorales.

Introduction

Concentration techniques in stool examination are used to increase the yield of detecting parasites (ova, cysts, larvae, trophozoites) by separating them from faecal debris. They are essential when parasite load is low. Two commonly used concentration methods are formalin-ether (ethyl acetate) sedimentation and zinc sulphate flotation.

Method 1 — Formalin-Ether Sedimentation (Ritchie's method)

  • Principle — formalin fixes & preserves parasites; ether/ethyl acetate dissolves lipids & debris, which float; parasites (heavier) sediment.
  • Procedure
    1. Emulsify ~1 g stool in 10 mL 10% formalin (sieves through gauze to remove debris).
    2. Add 3 mL ether (or ethyl acetate — safer); shake vigorously for 30 sec.
    3. Centrifuge at 500 g for 5 min.
    4. Four layers form: top (ether), debris plug, formalin layer, sediment (parasites).
    5. Decant supernatant; resuspend sediment; mount on slide with iodine or saline; examine under microscope.
  • Recovers — most ova, cysts, larvae, coccidia (Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora, Isospora), tapeworm eggs.
  • Does NOT recover — trophozoites (formalin distorts them); live parasites (formalin kills).
  • Advantage — broad spectrum; good for operculated eggs; preserves morphology.

Method 2 — Zinc Sulphate Flotation (Faust's method)

  • Principle — ZnSO₄ solution (specific gravity 1.18–1.20) is denser than most parasite eggs & cysts → they float to surface; heavy debris sinks.
  • Procedure
    1. Emulsify stool in tap water; filter through gauze.
    2. Add ZnSO₄ solution (33% w/v, SG 1.18).
    3. Centrifuge at 500 g for 2 min, or let stand 10 min (gravity).
    4. Carefully collect surface film with wire loop or coverslip.
    5. Mount on slide with iodine; examine.
  • Recovers — most nematode eggs (Ascaris, hookworm, Trichuris), cestode eggs (Taenia, Hymenolepis), protozoan cysts (Giardia, Entamoeba).
  • Does NOT recover — operculated eggs (Clonorchis, Opisthorchis, Diphyllobothrium, Paragonimus — they sink); unfertilised Ascaris eggs; trophozoites; heavy eggs (Schistosoma — some).
  • Advantage — cleaner preparation; cysts/eggs well-preserved; rapid.
  • Disadvantage — distortion of cysts if left too long; misses operculated eggs.

Other Concentration Methods

  • Brine flotation (saturated NaCl) — for Ascaris, hookworm (cheap; no centrifuge needed).
  • Baermann's technique — for Strongyloides larvae (warm water stimulates migration).
  • Harpant-Mori (acid-ether concentration) — for operculated eggs (Schistosoma).
  • Kato-Katz thick smear — quantitative (eggs per gram of stool) for Schistosoma & soil-transmitted helminths in epidemiological surveys.
  • Modified acid-fast stain — for Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora, Isospora.
  • Sedimentation for Schistosoma haematobium — urine (not stool).

Clinical Pearl

For a single stool sample, perform both direct wet mount (saline + iodine — detects trophozoites) and concentration technique (formalin-ether sedimentation — recovers most ova & cysts). Multiple samples (3 on alternate days) increase sensitivity because parasites shed intermittently (e.g., Giardia cysts pass in pulses). For suspected Strongyloides, use Baermann's technique or culture on nutrient agar (larval tracks visible). For Cryptosporidium in HIV patients with chronic diarrhoea, use modified acid-fast stain (Kinyoun) — pink oocysts (4–6 µm) against blue background. For Schistosoma haematobium, examine urine (terminal drops — contain eggs); for S. mansoni & S. japonicum, examine stool. Always provide the lab with relevant clinical history — immunocompromised status, travel, occupation (farmers — hookworm; fish handlers — Clonorchis, Opisthorchis).

IgM Pentamer (900 kDa) + J chain; 10 binding sites; largest Ig Most potent complement activator (classical pathway — single IgM can activate C1q; ~1000× more efficient than IgG); first Ig produced in primary immune response; agglutination (efficient — 10 binding sites); marker of acute/recent infection (IgM appears first)
IgA Dimer (secretory IgA) + J chain + secretory component; monomer in serum Mucosal immunity — protects respiratory, GI, GU tract, breast milk, saliva, tears; neutralises pathogens at mucosal surface without causing inflammation; provides passive immunity to neonate via colostrum/breast milk
IgE Monomer; binds FcεRI on mast cells & basophils with high affinity Type I (immediate) hypersensitivity — triggers mast cell degranulation (histamine, leukotrienes); defence against parasitic helminths (eosinophil-mediated ADCC)

Clinical Pearl

IgM is the diagnostic marker of acute infection — appears first (within 5–7 days), peaks at 1–2 weeks, disappears by 6–8 weeks. Detection of specific IgM (e.g., rubella IgM, dengue IgM, hepatitis A IgM, CMV IgM, EBV VCA IgM) indicates current or recent infection. IgG indicates past infection or vaccination — persists for years. In neonates, elevated IgM is abnormal — maternal IgG crosses placenta, IgM does not; fetal/neonatal IgM indicates congenital infection (TORCH — toxoplasma, rubella, CMV, HSV, syphilis, HIV, parvovirus B19). IgA deficiency is the most common primary immunodeficiency (1 in 500) — often asymptomatic but predisposes to recurrent sinopulmonary & GI infections (especially Giardia). Hyper-IgM syndrome (CD40L deficiency) — high IgM, low IgG/IgA/IgE — due to failed class-switching. Waldenström macroglobulinaemia — monoclonal IgM causing hyperviscosity syndrome.
q1_0_3_4:
Definition

High-level disinfectants (HLDs) are chemical agents that destroy all vegetative bacteria (including mycobacteria), viruses, fungi, and some bacterial spores (with prolonged contact — become sterilants). They are used for semi-critical items (contact mucous membranes or non-intact skin — endoscopes, respiratory therapy equipment, vaginal specula, laryngoscope blades) per Spaulding classification.

Two High-Level Disinfectants

1. Glutaraldehyde 2% (Cidex)

  • Properties — colourless liquid; activated by alkalising to pH 7.5–8.5; reuse for 14–28 days (check MRC ≥1.5% with test strip).
  • Action — alkylates proteins, nucleic acids → cell death.
  • Exposure — 20–45 min for HLD; 10 h for sterilisation.
  • Uses
    • Flexible endoscopes (gastroscope, colonoscope, bronchoscope).
    • Respiratory therapy equipment, anaesthesia equipment.
    • Laryngoscope blades, vaginal specula.
    • Dialysers, blood tubing.
    • Rubber & plastic items that cannot be autoclaved.
  • Limitations — irritant vapour (use closed container, PPE); fixes protein (must pre-clean items); inactivated by organic matter; M. chelonei outbreak risk if reused too long; not sporicidal at short exposure.

2. Ortho-Phthalaldehyde (OPA) 0.55%

  • Properties — clear pale-blue liquid; no activation needed; less irritating vapour; faster action; reuse for 14 days.
  • Exposure — 12 min for HLD at 20 °C; 6 h for sterilisation.
  • Uses
    • Replacement for glutaraldehyde — endoscopes, respiratory therapy equipment.
    • Manual & automated endoscope reprocessors.
  • Limitations — stains skin/proteins grey (repeated exposure); sensitises urology staff (occupational asthma); higher cost.

Other HLDs

  • Hydrogen peroxide 7.5% — no toxic residue; for endoscopes & instruments.
  • Peracetic acid 0.2–0.35% — Steris System 1; single-use; for rigid endoscopes & surgical instruments.
  • Hypochlorite 1% (5000 ppm) — for blood spills; surfaces.

Spaulding Classification

  • Critical items (enter sterile tissue) — require sterilisation.
  • Semi-critical items (contact mucous membranes) — require HLD.
  • Non-critical items (contact intact skin) — require intermediate/low-level disinfection.

Clinical Pearl

The most important practical lesson: HLD reduces microbial load but does not sterilise. For instruments entering sterile tissue (critical items — surgical instruments, implants), only true sterilisation is acceptable. The biggest source of endoscope-related outbreaks is atypical mycobacteria (M. abscessus, M. chelonei) — they survive standard glutaraldehyde by forming biofilm in instrument channels. Prevention: (1) meticulous manual cleaning with enzymatic detergent before disinfection; (2) discard glutaraldehyde after 14 days; (3) use automated endoscope reprocessors with filtered water & 70% alcohol flush; (4) store endoscopes vertically in drying cabinet. For duodenoscopes (ERCP), FDA (2015) recommends EtO sterilisation or peracetic acid after HLD due to repeated MDR-organism outbreaks.

WHO Five Moments for Hand Hygiene

The WHO Five Moments (2009) define the 5 critical moments during patient care when hand hygiene must be performed. It is the single most effective measure to prevent healthcare-associated infections.

  1. Before touching a patient
    • Before any physical contact — shaking hands, helping patient move, taking pulse/BP, examination.
    • Why — protects patient from microbes on healthcare worker's hands.
  2. Before clean/aseptic procedure
    • Before dressing a wound, inserting IV/urinary catheter, preparing injection, oral care, drawing blood.
    • Why — protects patient from microbes (including own flora) entering sterile sites. Most critical moment — directly prevents CLABSI, CAUTI, SSI.
  3. After body fluid exposure risk
    • After any procedure with body fluids, mucous membranes, non-intact skin, wound dressings — drawing blood, changing dressing, handling bedpan, suctioning.
    • Why — protects healthcare worker & environment from patient-derived microbes.
  4. After touching a patient
    • After any physical contact — handshake, examination, helping move.
    • Why — protects healthcare worker & other patients.
  5. After touching patient surroundings
    • After contact with bed rails, IV pole, bedside table, monitor, door handle, BP cuff, chart.
    • Why — protects healthcare worker & other patients from microbes left on surfaces.

Hand Hygiene Methods

  • Alcohol-based handrub (ABHR) — preferred; 20–30 sec; 60–80% ethanol/isopropanol; for all 5 moments when hands not visibly soiled.
  • Soap & water — 40–60 sec; when hands visibly dirty; before eating; after toilet; suspected/confirmed C. difficile (alcohol does NOT kill spores); norovirus outbreak.
  • Surgical hand scrub — 2–5 min with chlorhexidine or povidone-iodine.

WHO Technique for Alcohol Handrub

  1. Apply 3–5 mL product.
  2. Palm to palm.
  3. Right palm over left dorsum & vice versa.
  4. Palm to palm with fingers interlaced.
  5. Backs of fingers to opposing palms with fingers interlocked.
  6. Rotational rubbing of left thumb clasped in right palm & vice versa.
  7. Rotational rubbing with clasped fingers of right hand in left palm & vice versa.
  8. Once dry — hands are safe.

Why Hand Hygiene Saves Lives

  • Healthcare workers' hands are the most common vehicle of cross-transmission in hospitals.
  • Compliance can reduce HAIs by 30–50%.
  • WHO estimates improving hand hygiene could save 5–8 million lives annually.
  • Cost-effective — alcohol handrub is cheaper than soap-and-water.
  • Reduces spread of multidrug-resistant organisms (MRSA, VRE, ESBL, CRE, CRAB, CRPA).

Clinical Pearl

The single most important lesson: alcohol-based handrub is the gold standard for routine hand hygiene (20 sec, faster, more effective, better tolerated) — except when hands are visibly dirty or spore-forming organisms (C. difficile, anthrax, norovirus) are suspected (then soap-and-water mandatory). Wearing the same pair of gloves for multiple patients is the most dangerous hand-hygiene violation — gloves do not protect the next patient. The 5 Moments framework has been adopted in >180 countries — most successful patient-safety intervention in history.
